## Q2
In the worst case, the smallest number of comparisons required by a comparison-based sorting algorithm is:

## Q2 - Options
(A) ⌈log n⌉
(B) ⌈log₂(n!)⌉
(C) ⌈log n(n − 1)⌉
(D) n

## Q2 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Sorting Algorithms & Sorting Complexity
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2026 (22 Jun, Shift 2) · Paper 2 · Q60

A comparison sort must distinguish among n! possible input orders. Its decision tree therefore needs at least n! leaves, so its worst-case height is at least ⌈log₂(n!)⌉ comparisons.

## Q5
Consider the following statements about heap sort algorithm:<br>
A. The MAX-HEAPIFY procedure which runs in O(lg n) time, is the key to maintaining the max heap property<br>
B. The BUILD-MAX-HEAP procedure, which runs in O(lg n) time, produces max-heap from an unordered input array<br>
C. The MAX-HEAP-INSERT, which runs in O(lg) time, implements the insertion operation<br>
D. The HEAP-INCREASE-KEY procedure runs in O(n lg n) time, to set the key of new node of its correct value

## Q5 - Options
(A) A, B only
(B) A, C only
(C) B, D only
(D) A, B, C, D

## Q5 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Sorting Algorithms & Sorting Complexity
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2023 (17 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q29

Evaluate each statement against the standard time complexities of the heap operations, exactly as printed.

- **A.** MAX-HEAPIFY runs in O(lg n) time — true. It sifts a node down at most the height of the heap, which is O(lg n), and this is exactly the operation that restores the max-heap property at one node.
- **B.** BUILD-MAX-HEAP does not run in O(lg n) time — false as printed. Building a heap from an unordered array by calling MAX-HEAPIFY on every internal node costs O(n) overall, not O(lg n).
- **C.** MAX-HEAP-INSERT runs in O(lg n) time — true. Inserting a new element means placing it at the end and sifting it up along one root-to-leaf path, which takes time proportional to the heap's height.
- **D.** HEAP-INCREASE-KEY does not run in O(n lg n) time — false as printed. Increasing a key and sifting it up one path costs O(lg n), not O(n lg n).

Only A and C hold up under the correct complexities, matching option A, C only.

The source deliberately prints B's complexity as O(lg n) and D's as O(n lg n), both of which depart from the standard CLRS bounds for these operations, so this is a spot-the-error question rather than a transcription slip. Judging each statement literally against the true complexities is the intended approach, and it produces a clean, unambiguous match with one of the four options.

## Q8
There are many sorting algorithms based on comparison. The running time of heapsort algorithm is O(n lg n). Like P, but unlike Q, heapsort sorts in place where (P, Q) is equal to

## Q8 - Options
(A) Merge sort, Quick sort
(B) Quick sort, insertion sort
(C) Insertion sort, Quick sort
(D) Insertion sort, Merge sort

## Q8 - Hint
**Answer:** D
**Topic:** Sorting Algorithms & Sorting Complexity
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q60

In-place sorting algorithms sort elements without requiring extra auxiliary storage proportional to the input size (requiring O(1) auxiliary space):

- Heapsort is strictly an in-place comparison sort.
- Insertion sort operates in-place using O(1) auxiliary memory, matching property P.
- Merge sort requires O(n) auxiliary array space for merging, meaning it is not in-place, matching property Q.

Hence, like Insertion sort, but unlike Merge sort, heapsort sorts in place.

## Q9
Which of the following is best running time to sort n integers in the range 0 to n² - 1?

## Q9 - Options
(A) O(lg n)
(B) O(n)
(C) O(n lg n)
(D) O(n²)

## Q9 - Hint
**Answer:** B
**Topic:** Sorting Algorithms & Sorting Complexity
**Source:** UGC NET Jun 2019 (24 Jun, Shift 1) · Paper 2 · Q71

Sorting n numbers in the range 0 to n^2 - 1 can be achieved in linear time using Radix Sort:

Representing numbers in base n:<br>
Each number requires at most d = 2 digits in base n because the maximum value is n^2 - 1.

Using Counting Sort as the stable sub-routine:<br>
Each digit pass takes O(n + n) = O(n) time.<br>
With d = 2 passes, total runtime is 2 \* O(n) = O(n).

This achieves linear O(n) execution time.
